analysis.one_liner: Bans members of Congress and their families from owning or trading individual stocks, requiring divestment or blind trusts.
analysis.headline: Despite bipartisan sponsorship, the bill never received a hearing, markup, or vote in any of the three House committees it was sent to, and died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would bar members of Congress, their spouses, and their dependent children from buying or selling individual stocks, commodities, futures, and similar investments. Members would have to sell those holdings or put them into an approved blind trust within 120 days, and would face a fine of at least a month's salary for each 30 days of noncompliance. It also raises the penalty for late reports under the existing STOCK Act and requires financial disclosures to be filed electronically and posted online in a searchable public database. It was never taken up by any committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary citizens: the people who make federal laws could no longer hold investments whose value rises or falls with the laws and policies they write. The bill also makes members' financial disclosures easier for the public to search online.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits members of Congress, their spouses, and dependent children from purchasing or selling individual stocks, commodities, futures, and comparable investments, with civil penalties for violations.

Requires members to divest covered holdings or place them in an approved qualified blind trust within 120 days, with the trustee required to sell the original holdings so the member no longer controls them.
Imposes a civil penalty of at least one month of the member's salary, repeated every 30 days, for continuing failure to divest or certify compliance.
Adds a $500 fine for each late transaction report required by the STOCK Act and requires financial disclosures to be filed electronically and posted online in a searchable, downloadable format.

analysis.who_pays: Members of Congress and their households, who would have to sell individual stock holdings or place them in blind trusts, and spouses whose jobs pay in company stock, who would lose that compensation channel. Wealth-management firms would handle the required trusts.
analysis.who_pays_short: Members of Congress and their households

drawbacks.text: The bill leaves significant carve-outs: holdings tied to a spouse's primary occupation, including board-service compensation, are excluded, so a member's household could still build conflicts of interest through a spouse's career.

Setting up and administering qualified blind trusts, which must be run by a financial institution, carries real costs and paperwork, and members could lose investment flexibility relative to peers outside Congress.
Enforcement rests with the House and Senate ethics offices themselves to notice, notify, and fine members, and the bill provides no independent prosecutor for the core divestiture requirement.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core ban directly targets a conflict of interest that sits with lawmakers themselves, and the main costs fall on members rather than the public. The spousal-occupation carve-outs are the largest gap an honest supporter would acknowledge, since they let household conflicts persist outside the letter of the ban, and enforcement depends on the same ethics offices that have historically moved slowly.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to three House committees the day it was introduced, none of them ever took it up, and it expired when the 118th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi (D-IL) introduced the bill on April 18, 2023, joined by Reps. Michael Cloud (R-TX), Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-NY), and Joe Neguse (D-CO) as original sponsors.
The same day it was referred to the House Administration, Oversight and Accountability, and Judiciary Committees, with no committee designated to lead consideration.
The bill attracted 12 cosponsors, 5 Republicans and 7 Democrats.
No hearing, markup, or floor vote ever occurred; the action history shows no activity after the initial referral, and the bill died at the end of the 118th Congress on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Incumbent members of Congress are better off: they kept the ability to hold and trade individual stocks and their households' portfolios, and avoided divestment or blind-trust costs and new fines. No one outside Congress bore any burden from the bill's failure to advance.

industries.industry: Incumbent members of Congress and their households
industries.note: The bill would force them to sell individual stocks or place them in blind trusts within 120 days, expose spousal holdings online, and fine them a month's pay per month of noncompliance. Keeping the status quo preserves their ability to trade investments affected by the laws they write.

Qualified blind trusts must be held by a financial institution, so the bill would steer members' divestment business to banks and trust companies. The effect is modest because the bill never advanced.

The ban would eliminate a small base of retail trading customers among roughly 535 members and their immediate families. The broader securities market is unaffected because diversified funds, Treasuries, and municipal bonds remain allowed.
